run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_218 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Database question answered: the configured MySQL/MariaDB source (target m0-otel-20260909, schema testdb) contains exactly two tables, holmes_eval_218 and orders. holmes_eval_218 holds one row (id=1, category 'eval_test') whose verification_code is HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2. For the slow-query question, the structural cause is visible and confirmed by an execution plan: orders has only a PRIMARY index on id, no index on customer_id, so 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345' is executed as a table scan with a filter (EXPLAIN ANALYZE: 'Filter: (orders.customer_id = 12345)' over 'Table scan on orders', cost=101, 1000 rows scanned). The predicate is highly selective in principle (638 distinct customer_id values over 1000 rows, at most 5 rows per customer), which is exactly the pattern where a customer_id index pays off. Two caveats keep this partial rather than supported: the observed execution took only about 0.36 ms total for the 1000-row table, so the reported slowness is not reproduced at the current data size, and the predicate matched 0 rows at query time (customer_id values range 2..1000, so 12345 does not exist in the current data). Cardinality/locking/concurrency behaviour of the MySQL server under production load was not checked.

claims.text: The database source contains two tables in schema testdb: holmes_eval_218 and orders.
holmes_eval_218 has columns id (int), category (varchar(50)), verification_code (varchar(100)), created_at (timestamp) and only a PRIMARY index on id.
The verification code stored in holmes_eval_218 is HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2 (row id=1, category 'eval_test', created_at 2026-11-23T18:23:49); that select returned one row.
Table orders contains 1000 rows and has columns id (int, primary key), customer_id (int), order_date (date), total_amount (decimal(10,2)), status (varchar(20)).
orders carries only one index, PRIMARY on id (BTREE, unique, cardinality 1000); SHOW INDEX FROM orders returned no index on customer_id.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 shows 'Filter: (orders.customer_id = 12345) (cost=101 rows=100)' applied over 'Table scan on orders (cost=101 rows=1000) (actual time=0.051..0.315 rows=1000 loops=1)', i.e. all 1000 rows are read and filtered rather than searched by index.
customer_id in orders has 638 distinct values spanning 2 to 1000, with at most 5 rows per customer, so a single-customer lookup is highly selective.

The reported slowness is not reproduced at the current data size: the same EXPLAIN ANALYZE executed in about 0.36 ms total (table scan 0.051..0.315 ms over 1000 rows) and the filter matched 0 rows (actual rows=0), because customer_id values in orders only range 2..1000.

The slowness is caused by the absence of a supporting index: because orders has no index on customer_id, every execution of SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 does a full table scan whose cost grows linearly with table size; this is cheap in the sampled 1000-row dataset but would be the dominant cost on a production-sized orders table.

Part of the cost may come from SELECT * fetching all five columns per returned row; an index on customer_id alone still requires row lookups for the non-indexed columns, so a composite or covering index (customer_id, then the projected columns) may be needed if the read volume, not the scan, dominates.

Add a secondary index on orders(customer_id) (optionally a composite e.g. (customer_id, order_date) or a covering index matching the projected columns) and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the plan switches from 'Table scan on orders' to an index range/ref lookup.

Replace SELECT * with an explicit column list so the query can be served by a covering index, and add LIMIT/pagination if multiple orders per customer are expected (up to 5 rows per customer in the sampled data).

gaps: The reported production slowness was not reproduced: on the queried database the plan executes in ~0.36 ms over 1000 rows, so the environment/table size where the slow execution was observed is unknown.

customer_id 12345 does not exist in the current orders data (values range 2..1000, actual rows=0), so the plan for a high-cardinality/hot customer value and the returned row volume of the real workload are unknown.

MySQL server-side performance signals for the slow period (per-query statistics, buffer pool, I/O, lock waits, concurrent connections) are not available through the read-only SQL tools used here and were not checked.
Whether the query is executed with different literal values, joins or under concurrent load in the application was not observable from this Run.
The change_history integration is not available in this Run, so no conclusion can be drawn about when/whether an index was dropped or the schema changed.
Values in holmes_eval_218 were read at query time only; holmes_eval_218 was shown to contain one visible row, and any state during the authorized incident window is not verifiable from these reads.
next_steps: Enable/query MySQL performance_schema (e.g. events_statements_summary_by_digest) or the slow query log on the production instance to confirm the actual latency and rows_examined for this digest before changing schema.

Validate the proposed index on a replica: compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/after for SELECT customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? and confirm no duplicate/overlapping index already exists in production.
Check the production customer_id value distribution and hot-customer pattern, since 12345 is absent from the sampled data and the real selectivity may differ.

Correlate the slow-query reports with the application's order-lookup code path (optional DB tracing/metrics) to confirm the table scan is the dominant cost rather than network, connection-pool or lock contention.
